Need to search first.I've written notes for most of Psalm 119:89–117, but verses 102, 103, 107, 108 and 115–117 have no notes. I hit the tool's usage limit partway through, so I only read about 15 pages. Several were search-result excerpts rather than full pages, and none of them commented on those verses. I didn't find any material on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage, or any real arguments between Protestant traditions over it. Where a page I saw didn't say who wrote a comment, I say that.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview (vv. 89–96)**
- The section starts a new division of the psalm, under the Hebrew letter Lamed (Barnes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Guzik's heading for the section is "Saved by the word settled in heaven." He says these verses put God's word outside the created world and make it more lasting than creation, which makes sense because the world was made and is kept going by that word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Constable: God has kept his word safe in heaven (vv. 89–91). Because the writer delighted in that word, he could overcome his trouble (vv. 92–95). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-89.html
- Bridgeway: God and his word don't change and his promises are sure (vv. 89–91), so the psalmist trusts God to save him through his trials (vv. 92–96). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-89.html

**v. 89**
- Barnes: the Hebrew word for "settled" means to set or place something, like a pillar, altar or monument. Whatever God has made law stays law, and whatever he has promised is sure forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: God's word stays firm through every change (they link 1 Pet 1:25). It stands as firmly as the heaven it lives in and came from. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: because the word's home is heaven, it shares heaven's steadiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Calvin rejects the reading that the steadiness of the sky proves God is true. Because the earth is full of disorder, the psalmist places God's truth in heaven, where nothing changes, so believers can "fix their anchor there." https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- An unattributed excerpt on the same Bible Hub page mentions a Syriac reading, "for ever thou art, O Lord; and thy word stands," and applies the verse to Christ, the eternal Word, who has returned to heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Spurgeon's *Treasury of David* quotes J. M. Good, who took the Hebrew verb as a military term for drawing up an army's ranks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_089-096.cfm
- GotQuestions: "settled" means fixed and stable. God's word is eternal and can't change (it cites Isa 40:8 and Jas 1:17). https://www.gotquestions.org/your-word-is-settled-in-heaven.html

**v. 90**
- Calvin: the earth is unsettled, yet clear evidence of God's truth still shows on it. The firmness of his word isn't limited to heaven, and the earth stays as God set it up. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- Matthew Henry: the promises of God's covenant are fixed more firmly than the earth itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- *Treasury of David* (quoted writers): God's word and God's works are alike in being constant. Nature's dependability is a guarantee that his promises are dependable too. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_089-096.cfm

**v. 91**
- Calvin: the whole order of nature depends on God's decree alone. Calling everything God's "servants" is a strong way of saying it all obeys him. People who doubt or defy God resist the very faithfulness that holds creation together. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- Coffman notes that Leupold takes "they" to mean heaven and earth. Coffman prefers the ASV margin, "As for thy ordinances, they abide this day." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-89.html
- Keil & Delitzsch weigh Hitzig's reading against one in which all things "take their stand" ready to serve God's judgments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Matthew Henry: every creature does what it was made for, so man, the only one given reason, shouldn't be the only useless one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm

**v. 92**
- Calvin: the psalmist speaks from experience. The only comfort in trouble is resting on God's word and the grace and assurance of salvation it offers. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- Pulpit Commentary (S. Conway): without God's steady love, which filled him with delight, the psalmist couldn't have survived. The Holy Spirit writes the word on the heart. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-89.htm

**v. 93**
- Matthew Henry: the word without God's grace wouldn't give us new life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- *Treasury of David* (quoted writers): God gave the life, but through the word "soundly preached, savingly understood" and applied to the conscience. Comforted by the word, the psalmist pledges never to forget it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_089-096.cfm
- Conway: once someone has been revived by the word, memory and heart hold on to it. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-89.htm

**v. 94**
- Calvin: the psalmist argues from being God's own "stamp and coinage." That status comes only from God's free adoption, not human effort, and keeping the commands is evidence of it. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- *Treasury of David*: "I am Yours" shows a heart glad to belong to the Lord rather than to itself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_089-096.cfm
- Conway: this is complete self-surrender, and "save me" carries confidence that God will. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-89.htm

**v. 95**
- Calvin: this verse shows why he needs saving. Thinking hard on God's testimonies holds him up against attacks, calms fear and keeps him from bad advice. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- Conway: such meditation is an "antidote to all fear." https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-89.htm

**v. 96**
- Keil & Delitzsch: every earthly perfection ends, because at its peak it turns into its opposite. God's commandment is unlimited in how long it lasts and how far it proves true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- Calvin: this repeats v. 89. The word stands far above the world's perishing parts. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_89-96.htm
- Matthew Henry: the word fits every case and every time, and it turns us from trusting ourselves to Christ alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-89.htm
- *Treasury of David* (quoted writers) gives two readings:
  - Our sense of falling short comes from how perfect the Law is.
  - "I've seen the end of perfection in myself," yet the perfect command promises that God will one day make us what it describes.

  A third quoted writer says God's law reaches every thought and feeling. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_089-096.cfm
- GotQuestions: the verse shows God's word reaching across all space and time. https://www.gotquestions.org/your-word-is-settled-in-heaven.html

**v. 97**
- Guzik: the love is present tense, not "I used to" or "one day I will," and the psalmist is speaking about himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- GotQuestions cites this verse as a reason to meditate on Scripture. https://www.gotquestions.org/lamp-to-my-feet.html

**v. 99**
- *Treasury of David* (quoted writer): a godly preacher's student may end up passing him, as Augustine did his teacher Ambrose. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tod/psalms-119.html
- A sermon excerpt: because he obeyed, the psalmist gained more wisdom than his teachers. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-89.htm

**v. 105**
- Barnes: the word is like a torch on a dark night. It keeps a traveller from stumbling, falling or wandering off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-105.htm
- Calvin: the law was the psalmist's "schoolmaster" for holy living, set against all human advice. Without it, life is darkness. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_105-112.htm
- Gill: the word shows sin and our need of a better righteousness than our own, and it is the standard for faith and life. A lamp is useless to a blind man, so the Spirit must open the eyes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-105.htm (Gill's name is confirmed at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-105.html)
- Matthew Henry: the commandment is a lamp kept burning with "the oil of the Spirit." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-105.htm
- An unattributed excerpt: the lamp isn't the sun; it guides us until the "Sun of Righteousness" comes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-105.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: life's road runs through darkness past steep drops, and the word is both his torch and his sun. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-105.html
- Spurgeon: Scripture is not sent to dazzle us but to guide daily life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_105-112.cfm
- *Biblical Illustrator*: hold the lamp low, because it's for the feet, not for curious ideas. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-105.html
- GotQuestions: the Hebrew *ner* was a small clay lamp with one wick (it compares Prov 6:23 and 2 Pet 1:19). https://www.gotquestions.org/lamp-to-my-feet.html

**v. 106**
- Calvin: believers' vows rest on God's grace, which gives strength by the Holy Spirit, not on their own ability. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_105-112.htm
- An unattributed excerpt applies the verse to Christians as people "sworn in" by baptism and the Lord's Supper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-105.htm

**vv. 109–110**
- *Treasury of David* (quoted writer): Augustine admitted he didn't understand "life in my hands," but Jerome explained it as a Hebrew idiom for extreme danger. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tod/psalms-119.html
- A sermon excerpt: that kind of danger usually drives out holy thoughts, yet here he calmly remembers God's word, and the snares fail. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-105.htm

**vv. 111–112**
- Calvin: true obedience starts in the heart, and forced obedience "differs little from rebellion." "To the end" shows he kept going against every obstacle. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_105-112.htm

**vv. 113–114**
- Guzik: his hope wasn't just head knowledge; it rested on a relationship with God himself, his "hiding place and shield." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Matthew Henry (vv. 113–120): the more we love God's law, the more we watch against "vain thoughts." That phrase reflects the KJV wording of v. 113. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions
I found no real disagreement on these verses. The only points of different emphasis:
- **Reformed:** Calvin on v. 94 stresses free adoption, not merit (link above). On v. 105 he attacks the Catholic view that Scripture is obscure (see section 3).
- **Wesleyan:** Seedbed says not to look for a big difference between "lamp" and "light" in v. 105, since it's poetry for singing. It points beyond the written word to Christ, the "word made flesh," who is himself the path. https://seedbed.com/the-light-of-the-world-psalm-119105-128-nun-samekh-and-ayin/
- **Experience-focused:** Conway (Pulpit) on v. 93 says creeds, rituals and sacraments have proved weak, and only real experience of God's reviving holds a person. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-89.htm

## 3. Other views
**Catholic and Orthodox (Augustine, who uses the Latin numbering, Psalm 118)**, all at https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801119.htm
- **v. 90:** the "generations" may mean two eras, the Law and Prophets, and the Gospel.
- **v. 96:** the "consummation" means striving for the truth even to death, which ends in Christ's endless kingdom.
- **v. 97:** you can't love what God commands without loving the command itself.
- **v. 101:** he reads the psalm as the voice of Christ and his body, the Church. Christ, the Head, had no evil desires to hold back. Believers keep from evil because the Spirit wrote the law on their hearts, so they love it "as a son," not fear it as a slave.
- **v. 104:** keeping the commandments brings richer understanding.
- **v. 105:** the lamp is a created thing, lit by sharing in the eternal light.

**Catholic translation and Calvin's objection**
- The Douay-Rheims reads v. 96 as "an end to all persecution." https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-96.htm
- Calvin argues that v. 105 refutes the claim of "the Papists" that Scripture is obscure. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_119_105-112.htm

**Modern translation**
- The NET Bible renders v. 96 as "your commands are beyond full comprehension." I didn't reach its translators' note. https://www.blueletterbible.org/verse/net/psa/119/96/

**Popular modern teaching:** none found.

To fill the gaps, the next pages to read are Enduring Word's full sections on vv. 97–104 (Mem) and vv. 113–120 (Samek), Bible Hub's commentary pages for vv. 102–103, 107–108 and 115–117, and Augustine's later sections (Nun and Samekh).
